analysis.one_liner: Revises labor law to make union organizing harder and shield franchisors from joint liability.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2023 with 88 Republican cosponsors but never received a hearing or a vote, dying in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite federal labor law in several ways at once. It would narrow the standard for when two companies count as a single "joint employer" responsible for the same workers, expressly shield franchise companies from being treated as the employer of workers at their franchisees, require union elections to be conducted by secret ballot, restrict the personal contact information unions may use to reach workers during organizing drives, require employees to opt in annually before their union dues can be spent on anything beyond bargaining, and exempt tribal enterprises from federal labor law. The changes would make it harder for workers to form unions and easier for companies to avoid responsibility for wages and conditions at franchised or subcontracted workplaces.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially franchisors and large franchise chains, gain the most: a narrow joint-employer standard and the explicit carve-out for franchisors would keep national brands from being held responsible for wages and working conditions at franchise locations, and would limit collective liability when staffing agencies or contractors are involved. Businesses facing union drives also gain from the stricter secret-ballot requirement, the tight limits on contact information for union organizers, and the annual opt-in requirement that would shrink the dues unions can spend beyond bargaining.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Franchisors, employers, and businesses resisting unions

how_it_helps.text: Requires that a union be selected by secret ballot in an election conducted by the National Labor Relations Board.

Limits the personal information employers must hand unions during an organizing drive to one contact method chosen by each employee in writing, and makes it an unfair labor practice for unions to use that information for anything other than the election or to keep it afterward.
Requires employees to authorize in writing, with 35 days' notice and annual renewal, any use of their union dues for purposes beyond collective bargaining or contract administration.

analysis.who_pays: Workers pay: employees trying to organize would face tighter rules and less ability to reach coworkers, and workers at franchises and staffing arrangements would have a harder time holding the company that controls their jobs accountable for pay and conditions. Union treasuries would shrink as dues for political and organizing activity require yearly written renewal.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers seeking unions and joint-employer protections

drawbacks.text: The opt-in requirement for union dues spent on anything beyond bargaining, with re-authorization every year and no automatic renewal, would sharply cut union political and organizing funds — unions report that periodic re-authorization drives would reduce member participation.

The narrow joint-employer standard, plus the explicit bar on treating franchisor policies on harassment, paid leave, or childcare as evidence of joint employment, would make it harder for workers at franchises, staffing agencies, and subcontractors to hold the company that actually sets their working conditions responsible for wage theft, unsafe conditions, or retaliation.
Exempting tribal enterprises from federal labor law strips collective bargaining rights from workers at those businesses, though it is framed as respect for tribal sovereignty.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles a few privacy protections for union-election voters with provisions that would make it materially harder for workers to form unions and bargain (stricter secret-ballot requirement, tighter joint-employer standard, and opting annual re-authorization for any union political spending). The privacy and tribal-sovereignty pieces are limited and could have been advanced separately; the core effect shifts bargaining power toward employers and away from employees. Because it never received a hearing or vote, none of these trade-offs were tested in the legislative process.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Introduced April 19, 2023 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, its only committee referral.
It drew 88 Republican cosponsors — no Democrats — within the 118th Congress.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the initial referral and the sponsor's introductory remarks.
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025 without the bill ever reaching a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers — particularly franchise networks and businesses that would have faced joint-employer liability — are better off that it died, since it never constrained labor rules; workers lost a chance to have the privacy provisions considered, but the bill's core effect would have weakened unions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and franchise chains; unions avoided restrictions

for.name: Rep. Rick W. Allen
for.role: U.S. Representative (R-GA), bill sponsor and chair of the Workforce Protections Subcommittee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 19, 2023 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 88 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrats cosponsored.

sides.party_line_note: All 88 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and it never advanced far enough to produce a roll-call vote.

industries.note: The bill narrows how unions are recognized, restricts use of dues to purposes a member affirmatively authorizes each year, and limits the contact information unions may use in organizing drives — all of which shrink union membership, revenue, and reach.

The bill locks in a narrow joint-employer standard and explicitly shields franchisors from joint liability even when they require franchisees to adopt policies on harassment, paid leave, or childcare, insulating national brands from liability for labor violations at franchise locations.

industries.industry: Employers generally (including staffing and subcontracting firms)
industries.note: A narrower joint-employer standard and stricter union-selection rules reduce the risk of joint liability and make unionization harder, lowering labor costs at the expense of worker bargaining power.
